topics.title: Composite Functions
topics.subject: mathematics
outcomes: Understand and use function notation. (k, u, s)
Describe and understand a composite function. (k, u, s)
Work out the inverse of a function and recognise the graphical relationship between a function and its inverse. (k, u, s)

body.text: Function notation f(x) means "the rule f applied to x". If f(x) = 6x, then f(3) = 6(3) = 18. A composite function g(f(x)), written gf(x), means apply f first, then apply g to the result.

Given f(x) = 6x and g(x) = x+5: gf(3) means apply f then g. f(3)=18, then g(18)=18+5=23. Note the order matters — fg(3) means apply g first: g(3)=3+5=8, then f(8)=6(8)=48. gf(3) ≠ fg(3), so composite functions are not generally interchangeable in order.

The inverse of a function f, written f⁻¹, undoes what f does: if f(3)=18, then f⁻¹(18)=3. For f(x)=6x, work out the inverse by writing y=6x, swapping x and y to get x=6y, then solving for y: y=x/6, so f⁻¹(x) = x/6. Checking: f⁻¹(f(3)) = f⁻¹(18) = 18/6 = 3, correct.
Graphically, a function and its inverse are mirror images of each other in the line y=x — reflecting the graph of f(x) in that line gives the graph of f⁻¹(x).
